paragraphs.text: activities that can lead to trauma, as well as biopsies and surgical manipulations, all of which can exacerbate the ossifications [78, 92, 95–97].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders with Heterotopic Ossifications (HOs): Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) and Osteoma Cutis (OC)—iPPSD2, OMIM #166350

paragraphs.text: Because POH is due to a disrupted pater nal allele, there are no manifestations of hor monal resistance, and obesity is not present. Multiple AHO features have not been reported to occur in addition to the ossifications [97], and most often there are no other signs of AHO. As one would imagine, this makes the definitive diagnosis in infants and young chil dren difficult since even in PHP1A and PPHP, the AHO features are often not discernible at a young age. Therefore, one is often in a quan dary as to whether a child has PHP1A, PPHP, or POH when presenting with HOs at a young age unless an imaging study reveals that the HOs are penetrating. Therefore, any infant or child with HOs must be watched closely since the diagnosis is often an evolving one. One clinical feature that is helpful is that patients with POH are typically lean [38, 40, 42, 44]. In addition, as in PPHP, patients with POH often have intrauterine growth retardation and are born SGA [37, 38, 40–43, 80, 96, 97]. Rarely, POH can occur in a combined, over lapping syndrome along with PHP1A for which the etiology is an enigma, although it is possible that specific, yet unidentified GNAS mutations can lead to more invasive ossifica tions or that mosaicism may be involved, especially in light of the dermatomyotomal pattern of the ossifications in some patients [98, 99].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders with Heterotopic Ossifications (HOs): Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) and Osteoma Cutis (OC)—iPPSD2, OMIM #166350

paragraphs.text: OC is a condition that is also due to inac tivating mutations on the paternal GNAS allele encoding Gαs. However, in OC, the SCOs are present in isolation without any other clinical features of AHO or POH and without hormonal resistance or obesity as in PHP1A. The ossifications are always limited to the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and do not cross fascial planes. Although OC itself is benign, it can be the initial presenting sign of PPHP before the development of other mani festations of the clinical phenotype of AHO. Similarly, it can represent the initial clinical sign of POH before the development of penetrating HOs. Even though OC is due to paternally inherited GNAS mutations, just
paragraphs.heading: Disorders with Heterotopic Ossifications (HOs): Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) and Osteoma Cutis (OC)—iPPSD2, OMIM #166350

paragraphs.text: like PPHP and POH, OC can also be mis taken as an early form of PHP1A before there are overt AHO findings or evidence of hor monal resistance and obesity [37, 38, 40, 78, 100–102]. Therefore, OC must be monitored closely for its potential evolution into more serious conditions. As in the other conditions, one should avoid removing the ossifications surgically.

paragraphs.heading: Affecting cAMP Signaling Downstream of GNAS: Acrodysostosis Type 1 (ACRDYS1)—iPPSD4, OMIM #101800 and Acrodysostosis Type 2 (ACRDYS2)—iPPSD5, OMIM #614613

paragraphs.text: nasal hypoplasia, facial dysostosis, maxillary hypoplasia, narrowed lumbar spine, and occa sionally shortened femoral necks. Other issues such as craniosynostosis, cranial hyperostosis, and CM1 can occur, as well as frequent otitis media. The bone age is often severely advanced [38, 41, 52, 55, 114]. Of importance is that these skeletal abnormalities can be accompa nied by hormonal resistance [52–55, 112–115]. Due to the skeletal features along with hor monal resistance, these patients are sometimes misdiagnosed as having PHP1A, and muta tion testing can be very helpful in this regard. Overall, however, the skeletal phenotype and short stature are more severe than in PHP1A. In rare cases, acrodysostosis can be caused by a mutation in GNAS.

paragraphs.text: As described in the preceding sections, the spectrum of pseudohypoparathyroidism and related disorders comprises a group of condi tions that have a unique yet overlapping set of clinical phenotypes. Additionally, many of these disorders have clinical signs, symptoms, and biochemical/hormonal profiles that change over the lifespan. In many cases, the diagnosis of these disorders can be narrowed down significantly based on family history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and imaging even before performing mutation analysis. However, as is evident throughout this chapter, patients with PHP and related disorders can have findings consistent with more than one condition. Therefore, genetic testing can be quite helpful in several respects.
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: First, in some cases, the clinical diagnosis can be inconclusive. This especially pertains to PHP and related disorders since the range
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: of phenotypes can be variable, both in terms of the age of onset of clinical and laboratory features as well as the severity of signs and symptoms. As discussed earlier, patients can sometimes be given a diagnosis consistent with one disorder, which is subsequently amended as additional clinical features develop or become apparent over time. Therefore, identification of the specific genetic alteration is important in order to confirm the diagnosis of the patient. Second, knowing the specific mutation can provide information for current and future family members since tar geted testing for the specific region of the affected gene can be performed if needed for their own evaluations or future evaluations; this saves both time and money as well. In this respect, prenatal diagnosis is also possible, and collaborations with geneticists and genetic counselors can be very helpful. Third, and important going forward into the future, genetic testing can reveal the severity of the mutation, which can be useful in a general sense in anticipating the severity of certain clinical features based on genotype-phenotype correlations, such as the correlation observed with subcutaneous ossifications [100]. Although genotype-phenotype correlations are not available for many of the clinical issues observed in PHP and related disorders, more of these correlations may evolve with the greater availability and sophistication of molecular testing over the past decade and with scientific investigations continually advancing.
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Genetic testing for diagnostic purposes is available for most of the PHP and related dis orders in multiple commercial CLIAapproved laboratories through targeted testing and sequencing of key genes, such as GNAS, PRKAR1A, PDE4D, and PDE3A, that are discussed in this chapter (for review, [38–43]). Methylation analysis, as well as test ing for STX16 deletions to confirm the diag nosis of PHP1B, can also be performed in CLIA-approved laboratories, although meth ylation testing is not always routinely avail able. A small percentage of sporadic PHP1B is due to patUPD20q, which can also be assessed. If determination of the parental ori
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: gin of the mutant allele is important for diag nostic purposes, a simple approach is to perform genetic testing on the parents or other family members. In cases in which this is not possible due to adoption or spontaneous mutations, analysis of the parental origin of the mutation from patient RNA can be per formed in a research laboratory for investiga tional purposes. Finally, although there are instances in which the diagnosis of these dis orders is identified by whole exome (or genome) sequencing, these tests are not typi cally needed for diagnostic purposes if a thor ough clinical workup has been completed, including a detailed history, physical examina tion, and laboratory/radiologic evaluation. However, on occasion, these more extensive analyses are truly necessary and can prove to be quite helpful.

Remarkable advances have been made toward understanding the mechanisms underlying the PHP spectrum ever since its initial descrip tion by Fuller Albright and colleagues approximately eight decades ago. Through both clinical and laboratory investigations, the phenotypes have been elucidated in more detail, and the mechanisms of the multiple clinical issues have been unfolding, such as for the multihormone resistance, adult short stat ure, brachydactyly, subcutaneous ossifica tions, obesity and metabolic disturbances, craniofacial and dental abnormalities, aber rant bone regulation, and cognitive/behav ioral impairments that are often a part of these conditions. As more knowledge has continually been gained from clinical and lab oratory investigations, the diagnosis, treat ment, and management for these patients have improved immensely, as has the aware ness of these conditions overall. Due to the evolving nature of the clinical issues in PHP and related disorders as well as their complex ities, constant attention to early intervention, close follow-up, and long-term management is key to the overall health and quality of life for patients with these conditions.

paragraphs.text: Part 1 Question 1: E PTH resistance is not always accompanied by low calcium and high phosphate levels, especially during childhood. The congeni tal hypothyroidism is an important piece of information; it is often a misdiagno sis and instead represents TSH resistance in an infant with PHP1A. If an infant or child is successfully treated with levothy roxine in the setting of congenital hypo thyroidism based on normalization of the thyroid function tests but continues to have excessive weight gain despite adequate treatment, then the possible diagnosis of PHP1A should be considered. The obesity in PHP1A is primarily caused by imprint ing in the dorsomedial hypothalamus, spe cifically in MC4R-expressing cells [given that the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) is Gαs-coupled]. The subcutaneous nod ules are heterotopic ossifications and not calcifications, and along with brachy dactyly should raise high suspicion for PHP1A. Children with PHP1A are often a normal height. Instead, PHP1A is charac terized by adult short stature.

paragraphs.text: Question 2: E Growth hormone stimulation testing should be the standard of care in PHP1A, regardless of the height, and it should be performed before the growth velocity decreases since GH deficiency occurs com monly with PHP1A. Bone age cannot be used to predict final adult height since it accelerates rapidly in light of the premature epiphyseal fusion that occurs due to accel erated chondrocyte differentiation. Even if the boy is GH sufficient, his adult height will be compromised. Part 2 Question 1: A, B, E The child either inherited the GNAS mutation from his mother, or he has a spontaneous mutation. Given the other information provided, it is clear that he has inherited the mutation. The mother has subcutaneous ossifications, a hall mark of PHP1A and PPHP. She has no other medical issues; therefore, she has PPHP. The mother is not overweight, which is also consistent with PPHP; obe sity is typical of PHP1A. The mother’s sister has brachydactyly and subcutane ous ossifications, and therefore, she also has PPHP. The mother and maternal aunt would have inherited the GNAS mutation from their father (maternal grandfather of patient) since PPHP is passed on by inheritance of a mutant paternal allele. It is extremely unlikely that the biologic maternal grandfather is unaffected since he had two daughters with PPHP. Part 3 Question 1: C The advanced bone age is indicative of PHP1A and represents premature epiphy seal fusion. It is not indicative of pubertal development. Hand/wrist bone age read ings are not helpful in PHP1A, and they tend to be more advanced than those for the knee.

Key Points

5 The main feature of pseudohypopara

thyroidism is defective signaling at the PTH/PTHrP receptor leading to endorgan resistance, often accompanied by impaired signaling of other G proteincoupled receptors along with their asso ciated hormonal resistances; downstream defects in cAMP signaling can lead to disorders resembling PHP. 5 Treatment of hormonal resistance is

crucial and needs to be monitored closely in several of the PHP and related disorders, such as for the resultant hypocalcemia, hypothyroidism, hypo gonadism, growth hormone deficiency, and obesity-related issues that can occur. 5 A careful physical examination is criti

cal to the diagnosis of PHP and related disorders: for example, brachydactyly and subcutaneous ossifications are hall marks of PHP1A and PPHP, and even in infancy, when brachydactyly may not be obvious, the identification of subcu taneous ossifications and early onset obesity can trigger the diagnosis of PHP1A, especially in an infant identi fied as having hypothyroidism on new born screening. 5 Because children with PHP1A have a

markedly increased risk of GH defi ciency but are often not short, it is important not to delay GH stimulation testing and potential treatment until growth has decelerated, especially in light of the premature epiphyseal fusion and absent pubertal growth spurt that lead to the adult short stature typical of the condition. 5 The medical issues along with the cog

nitive, behavioral, and developmental impairments that can occur in PHP and related disorders should involve early intervention as well as vigilant longterm management by a knowledgeable medical team equipped to provide the necessary support and advocacy for both the patients and their families.

### 22

### 22.1 Historical Background

The term pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) describes a group of disorders that have in common renal resistance to parathyroid hor mone (PTH) with consequent hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated serum levels of bioactive PTH. PHP was first characterized by Fuller Albright and col leagues in 1942 in a publication that described three unrelated patients with striking physical features who lacked the appropriate phospha turic response to the administration of para thyroid extract “in spite of the fact that larger and larger amounts were given [1].” They demonstrated that although the patients had evidence of biochemical hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, these patients failed to respond to exogenous parathyroid extract, leading the investigators to conclude that this was “not lack of para thyroid hormone but a failure of the organism to respond to it.” They hypothesized that these patients had end-organ resistance to PTH, and because they manifested the bio chemical features of hypoparathyroidism, they named this unusual variant “pseudohy poparathyroidism.”

In addition to the biochemical abnormali ties, Albright and his associates also noted that these patients manifested a unique con stellation of developmental features. The orig inal description revealed specific characteristics that included being “short and rather thick-set” and having a “very round face” with “metacarpal and metatarsal bones [that were] extremely short and stubby.” In addition, examinations of the patients revealed “marked density of the skull” with the “skeleton as a whole [being] abnormally dense,” multiple dental abnormalities, and subcutaneous ectopic ossifications described as “hard, calcified masses in the subcutaneous tissues.” Cognitive impairment was noted at varying levels with one described as “extremely” affected and another as “some what backward mentally.” However, aside from the hormone resistance, not all features were ubiquitously present in each individual patient [1]. Subsequent investigations by


## PDF page 565 | printed page 559

Albright and his colleagues over the next decade led to the publication in 1952 of a unique patient who presented with similar somatic features to PHP but who displayed normal calcium and phosphate levels and a normal phosphaturic response after adminis tration of parathyroid extract. They empha sized three unique findings in this patient that seemed consistent with PHP patients as well, including “(a) round faces and short, thick-set figures; (b) early epiphyseal closure of some of the metacarpal and metatarsal bones with resulting shortening of the involved fingers and toes; and (c) subcutaneous foci of ectopic ossification.” However, end-organ resistance to parathyroid extract was absent unlike in PHP. Therefore, Albright and his colleagues referred to this new disorder as “pseudopseu dohypoparathyroidism” (PPHP) because the condition resembled PHP in having the same somatic features but lacked evidence of hor monal resistance [2]. These developmental characteristics were later collectively termed “Albright hereditary osteodystrophy” (AHO). Subsequently, other patients were described who had PTH resistance but lacked features of AHO [3, 4], thus further extending the complexity of the disorder.

In the late 1960s, with the discovery that cyclic AMP (cAMP) produced by adenylyl cyclase was the second messenger for many hormones, Gerald Aurbach and colleagues began studies that would ultimately identify the molecular basis for PTH resistance in PHP [5, 6]. They showed first that cAMP was the second messenger for PTH in the kidney and second that the absent phosphaturic response to PTH in PHP was associated with a markedly blunted increase in urinary excre tion of cAMP. These observations implicated a failure of PTH to stimulate the enzyme ade nylyl cyclase in the kidney as the basis for hor mone resistance. PHP patients with defective cAMP and phosphaturic responses to PTH were termed PHP type 1 (PHP1) to distin guish them from patients with PHP type 2 (PHP2) who lacked features of AHO and in whom PTH administration elicited an appro priate increase in urinary excretion of nephrogenous cAMP but failed to induce a

phosphaturic response [3, 7]. Key investiga tions published in 1980 by Michael Levine, Henry Bourne, and others revealed that patients with PHP with concomitant features of AHO had a 50% reduction in Gαs bioactiv ity utilizing in vitro assays of extracts from human erythrocyte membranes whereas those without AHO had normal or minimally diminished activity [8, 9]. With that discovery came a revised nosology for PHP1: those with reduced Gαs bioactivity with AHO features were referred to as having PHP1A, whereas those with overall normal Gαs bioactivity but without AHO features were said to have PHP1B. This molecular dichotomy led to a further refinement in the endocrine phenotype of PHP1 such that resistance to multiple hor mones whose receptors required Gαs to acti vate adenylyl cyclase was a feature of PHP1A [10, 11] while isolated PTH resistance was typical of PHP1B [12].

By the late 1980s, the ability to assay PTH accurately from direct measurements in patients was available [13], and by 1990, the first mutations in GNAS, the gene encoding Gαs, were identified as being the cause of PHP1A and PPHP [14, 15]. Soon after this major discovery, a greater understanding of the complexities of PHP and its related disor ders began to unfold, and a search for the eti ology of PHP1B was underway [16–20] (for review, [21]). Concomitantly over this period of time, the distinction between PHP1A and PPHP was found to be a manifestation of the parental origin of the defective GNAS allele, and with further delineation of the regulation of the highly complex GNAS locus, the basis for this unusual pattern of inheritance was determined to be paternal imprinting of GNAS [22–27]. During this time, investiga tions on mouse models not only demonstrated that the Gnas locus was regulated by a highly complex system of reciprocal imprinting but also showed that hormone resistance in spe cific tissues was related to a tissue-specific pat tern of paternal imprinting for Gαs [28, 29]. In the sections that follow, the further delinea tion of the mode of inheritance as well as the pathophysiologic processes uncovered by investigations in both humans and mice to

Advances are continually being made toward understanding the mechanisms under lying the PHP spectrum and related disorders, and through clinical and laboratory studies, the phenotypes are being more carefully eluci dated as are the etiologies of their clinical issues, such as hormone resistance, short stat ure, skeletal and craniofacial/dental abnor malities, heterotopic ossifications, obesity and metabolic disturbances, and cognitive/behav ioral impairments.

### 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

As alluded to above, PHP1A and PPHP with the associated AHO phenotype are caused by heterozygous inactivation of GNAS, the gene that encodes the α-stimulatory subunit (Gαs) of the heterotrimeric G protein, Gs, that cou ples heptahelical receptors (G protein-coupled receptors, GPCRs) for a large variety of hor mones and neurotransmitters to adenylyl cyclase [14, 15, 30–43]. Transmembrane signal transduction is initiated by the binding of agonist ligands to specific GPCRs (e.g., PTH in the case of the type 1 PTH receptor), which

leads to the dissociation of Gαs from the het erotrimeric αβγ Gs complex. Free Gαs binds to and activates adenylyl cyclase, while the βγ subunits can stimulate other signaling enzymes as well as some isoforms of adenylyl cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP, which activates a variety of downstream effec tors to produce the physiological responses to hormone stimulation. Levels of intracellular cAMP are regulated by the balance between the activities of adenylyl cyclase and cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase (PDE). A large number of genes encode a variety of isoforms for these two important enzymes, which vary in their patterns of tissue-specific expression and provide discrete mechanisms for generat ing cell-type and stimulus-specific responses to GPCR activation. The most well-studied of the effector targets of cAMP is protein kinase A (PKA), which regulates a variety of signaling pathways via phosphorylation of many metabolic enzymes and transcription factors. However, cAMP also regulates the activity of EPAC (a guanine-nucleotideexchange factor) and cyclic-nucleotide-gated ion channels.

Gαs is encoded by exons 1–13 of GNAS. Mutations can occur in any exon as well as intron/exon boundaries [57] and can be inher ited or occur spontaneously. The GNAS locus is highly complex given that it generates tran scripts for not only Gαs (exons 1–13) but also neuroendocrine secretory protein 55 (NESP55), extra-large alpha-stimulatory sub unit (XLαs), A/B (also called 1A), as well as an antisense transcript (AS). The A/B tran script may encode a truncated form of Gαs that can act in an inhibitory fashion, (for review, [21, 34–43]), [25, 27, 58–64]. The dif ferent transcripts are generated through the use of alternative first exons. The GNAS locus is controlled by genomic imprinting, which is regulated through differentially methylated regions (DMRs) that are within the promoter regions for each exon, except exon 1 of GNAS (which is part of the coding sequence for Gαs). The promoters for XLαs, AB, and AS are methylated on the maternal allele, thus lead ing to transcription predominantly from the paternal allele. Of note is that XLαs can act similarly to Gαs and even augment its action

[64, 65]. NESP55, on the other hand, is meth ylated on the paternal allele resulting in expression predominantly from the maternal allele [25, 27]. Imprinting is often partial and leads to transcriptional repression of one allele. In particular, expression of Gαs tran scripts from the paternal allele is suppressed in certain tissues, many of which are endo crine. This is termed “paternal imprinting” because there is inhibition of transcription of the paternal allele. In other tissues, imprinting does not occur, leading to biallelic expression of both the maternal and paternal alleles. The development of PHP1A versus PPHP is dependent on the parent-of-origin of the mutant allele and is due to this mechanism of imprinting, specifically determined to be due to tissue-specific paternal imprinting based on investigations in humans as well as mouse models. In tissues in which imprinting plays a role, the consequences on clinical phenotype can be very different between the two condi tions [28, 29, 66–74], whereas in those tissues in which imprinting does not play a promi nent role, the clinical phenotypes can be simi lar [22–29], (for review, [32, 34–38, 40–43]).

The presence or absence of hormonal resistance in association with AHO was first determined through clinical analysis of family pedigrees, which revealed that mothers affected with either PHP1A or PPHP had children with PHP1A, whereas fathers with either PHP1A or PPHP had children with PPHP. It was eventually determined that patients with PHP1A have GNAS mutations on their maternally inherited allele, and those with PPHP carry mutations on their pater nally inherited allele, which led to the discov ery of the mechanisms involved [22–27]. This unique mode of inheritance was confirmed in murine models with a targeted disruption of Gnas, which revealed tissue-specific silencing of Gαs expression from the paternal allele [28, 29, 66].

Because the normal paternally inherited GNAS allele in PHP1A patients is suppressed in imprinted tissues (many of which are endocrine-related), the loss of Gαs from the abnormal maternal allele results in a near complete absence of Gαs. The severe defi ciency of Gαs impairs GPCR signal transduc

By contrast, hormone respon siveness is normal in cells in which the paternal GNAS allele is active, as the loss of Gαs from the defective maternal allele results in only a 50% reduction in Gαs protein. As demon strated in investigations both in humans and in murine models, the imprinting is partial with only modest expression of Gαs from the paternal GNAS allele in the renal proximal tubules, thyroid follicular epithelial cells, gonad cells, and pituitary somatotropes, thereby causing multihormone resistance to PTH, TSH, LH/FSH, and GHRH, respec tively [28, 29, 66–74]. Calcitonin resistance has also been reported [34–43, 75, 76], and there is suggestive evidence in an AHO mouse model that partial imprinting in osteoclasts may affect bone remodeling due to calcitonin resistance [77, 78]. In contrast to PHP1A, patients with paternally inherited GNAS mutations develop PPHP and do not develop hormone resistance. They are often small-forgestational-age (SGA) at birth. This may be due to decreased XLαs, which is normally expressed from the paternal allele and is thought to be important in fetal growth [34, 79, 80].

In addition to hormone resistance, patients with PHP1A are typically obese, especially characterized by marked early-onset obesity starting soon after birth, whereas those with PPHP are not severely obese [44]. This obser vation changed the classic description of AHO that had previously been thought to include obesity. In addition, this noted differ ence in the obesity phenotype in PHP1A ver sus PPHP raised the possibility of imprinting in the hypothalamus given that the melano cortin-4 receptor (MC4R) is Gαs-coupled. Investigations in mice demonstrated no imprinting in adipose tissue [29, 81], and it was eventually determined through continued work on mouse models that imprinting occurs in the dorsomedial hypothalamus, specifically in MC4R-expressing cells [82, 83]. Human studies have also revealed the lack of imprint ing in adipose [84]. Therefore, the evidence supports hypothalamic imprinting as an underlying cause of the obesity such that

Although tissue-specific imprinting of GNAS leads to differences in the clinical phe notypes seen in PHP1A and PPHP, GNAS is biallelically expressed in other cell types and tissues, such as skin (fibroblasts), renal medulla, renal collecting ducts/ascending limb, adrenal, heart, nasal epithelia, lympho cytes, adipocytes, and chondrocytes, as has been demonstrated through both human and mouse investigations [11, 28, 29, 47, 66, 67, 70, 81, 84–90]. This biallelic expression results in clinical phenotypes that are shared between PHP1A and PPHP, specifically brachydactyly, shortened adult stature, and subcutaneous ossifications. These result from partial loss of Gαs activity in the specific cell types involved in which GNAS is biallelically expressed, such as chondrocytes in the case of brachydactyly and short stature. This would implicate that these phenotypes would be similar between PHP1A and PPHP because GNAS would be expressed equivalently in both.

Disorders besides PHP1A and PPHP can result from mutations in the GNAS locus. PHP1C presents clinically and biochemically in the same manner as PHP1A but is due to mutations that impair receptor coupling activ ity of Gαs but not its basal activity [26, 37–43]. It has been proposed by experts that PHP1C be removed from the nomenclature in the future [41, 42].

Other distinct conditions in the PHP spectrum that result from mutations in GNAS exons encoding Gαs specifically on the pater nal allele have heterotopic ossifications (HOs) as the predominant feature (for review, [34–43, 78]), [91–97]. One of these is progressive osse ous heteroplasia (POH), characterized by penetrating HOs as the main feature, typically without other physical features or hormonal resistance. There is also a very rare condition involving an overlap of both PHP1A and POH [98, 99], in which patients have features of both disorders. Finally, isolated osteoma cutis (OC) can occur, which is the clinical find ing of subcutaneous ossifications in isolation, also typically from mutations on the paternal

allele within the exons encoding Gαs. This can evolve into PPHP or POH over time (and even into PHP1A with hormonal resistance in rare circumstances when the SCOs are the only presenting sign and are inadvertently diag nosed as OC). POH and OC are typically caused by spontaneous mutations (unless the OC is representative of the early phase of PPHP and has been inherited) (for review, [34, 35, 37–43, 78]), [100–102].

Epigenetic defects within the GNAS gene cause PHP1B (for review [21, 30–43]), [19, 45–51]. All patients to date with PHP1B have a loss of methylation (LOM) within the Exon A/B DMR (specifically A/B:TSS-DMR) on the maternal GNAS allele. In most patients with familial PHP1B, the methylation defect is limited to LOM of exon A/B, but some cases of familial PHP1B and nearly all cases of sporadic PHP1B exhibit more extensive methylation defects that include LOM at the DMR for XLαs and gain of methylation (GOM) at the DMRs for NESP55. Approximately 15–20% of PHP1B is familial and due to maternal transmission of heterozy gous microdeletions within the maternal STX16 allele about 220 kb upstream of GNAS that include either STX16 exons 4–6 or exons 2–4, which presumably affect a cis-regulatory element that is important for methylation of the GNAS exon A/B DMR. The sporadic forms of PHP1B make up the majority of cases and tend to have more extensive meth ylation defects involving GNAS exon A/B:TSS-DMR and AS2:DMR in associa tion with methylation changes affecting vari ous alternative transcripts. Deletions within NESP and XL or paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q (patUPD20q) have been identified in some PHP1B patients with global methylation defects (for review, [21, 36–38, 41–43, 103, 104]), [45–50, 105–111].

Often a dimple is observed in place of the knuckle ( Figs. 22.1d and 22.3e).

These physical features are often a key to unlocking the diagnosis, particularly for patients with PPHP, who may have been unaware of these specific abnormalities because they had not been considered to be medically significant or because they had gone unnoticed. Indeed, a common scenario is that a mother brings her child with PHP1A to the clinic, and she is then noticed to have skeletal features of AHO, leading to the diagnosis of PPHP in the mother. have one or two digits that are out of propor tion in length to the others and undergo surgi cal intervention, which is not advised; the irregularity in sizes between the various fin gers and toes seems to be easily adapted to over time with proper management, such as with customized shoes and orthotics. Occupational and physical therapy as well as management by podiatry and specialized shoe stores can be of great benefit. In addition, the hand abnormalities predispose these patients to develop carpal tunnel syndrome, which has been documented as being at an increased prevalence in both children and adults with PHP1A and PPHP; the overall prevalence of carpal tunnel syndrome in AHO for patients of all ages is 67%; in children, the prevalence is 36% [125]. The symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome can mimic those of paresthesias secondary to hypocalcemia; therefore, it is important to follow up on these symptoms if the patient is normocalcemic, as early inter vention can prevent the need for surgery.

### 22.4.2.1 Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)

### Resistance

PTH resistance is the hallmark of pseudohy poparathyroidism and can lead to hypocalce mia and hyperphosphatemia. Because both hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathy roidism are characterized by hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, it is important to dif ferentiate these two entities. In hypoparathy roidism, there is insufficient production of PTH by the parathyroid glands, leading to low, undetectable, or inappropriately normal PTH levels. There is a normal response to the administration of PTH in terms of increased urinary excretion of cAMP and phosphate. In pseudohypoparathyroidism, on the other hand, there is end-organ resistance to PTH,

### 22

resulting in increased PTH levels, with a lack of response to PTH administration and a blunted or absent urinary excretion of cAMP and phosphate. Although PTH resistance clas sically manifests as the association of elevated PTH levels, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocal cemia, it must be diagnosed in the setting of normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D and magnesium levels, as well as normal renal function. Otherwise, the diagnosis is not definitive.

In PHP1A, the PTH resistance is often not present at birth but develops later in child hood, typically in the elementary school years (approximately 7–8 years of age) [37, 40, 41, 137]. A typical sequence is that the PTH eleva tion is accompanied by hyperphosphatemia initially and is then followed by hypocalcemia. The delay in the onset of PTH resistance in PHP1A is thought to be secondary to the pro gressive loss of GNAS expression in the proxi mal convoluted renal tubules due to paternal imprinting [28, 29, 67, 137, 138]. Because imprinting occurs only in the proximal tubules and not in the collecting ducts or ascending limb based on mouse models [28, 29, 67], it is thought that hypercalciuria is rarely observed in PHP1A since calcium reabsorption in the distal parts of the kidney is unaffected. As a result, nephrocalcinosis and renal stones are rarely seen. Renal ultrasounds are deemed necessary only if there is hypercalciuria or symptoms, although measuring a urine [calcium]:[creatinine] ratio is prudent at least once a year [34, 35, 38, 40, 139].

If PTH resistance is untreated, the PTH will continue to rise along with the phosphate, and hypocalcemia will ensue. Because the pro gression of hypocalcemia can be very gradual with adaptation to symptoms, patients can often present to the outpatient clinic with PTH levels in the 300 pg/mL range and serum calcium levels significantly below 2 mmol/L. In those patients previously undiagnosed, the initial presentation can sometimes be hypo calcemic seizures due to prolonged PTH resis tance leading to a gradual decline in calcium, which may be unnoticed until it reaches criti cally low levels. Therefore, it is of utmost importance that PTH resistance be diagnosed early and treated appropriately upon its pre sentation. In addition, over time, hyperphos

### 22.4.2.4 Growth Hormone-Releasing

### Hormone (GHRH) Resistance

In addition to premature fusion of the epiphy ses, another contributing factor to adult short stature in PHP1A is GH deficiency as a result of GHRH resistance secondary to partial imprinting of GNAS in the pituitary, specifi cally causing a deficient response in pituitary somatotropes [71]. GH deficiency occurs in approximately 70% of patients with PHP1A [34, 40, 72, 73, 127], and it is usually partial, although severe deficiency can be observed. It is important to reiterate that most children with PHP1A are NOT short. Therefore, GH deficiency needs to be considered even if chil dren are of normal or tall stature. Because GH deficiency is so common, it is standard of care to perform GH stimulation testing in all patients with PHP1A [34, 38, 40, 42, 72, 127, 148]. Treatment with recombinant growth hormone (rGH) is within approved guidelines for those who are found to be GH-deficient [38, 40, 72, 127, 149]. Testing for GH status, as well as rGH treatment for GH-deficient PHP1A patients (provided that there are no risk factors), is also currently supported by the international Consensus Statement, for which experts worldwide established uniform guidelines for management of pseudohypo parathyroidism [38] (also reviewed in [40–42]).

The mean adult height of untreated GH-deficient adults with PHP1A is signifi cantly shorter than for PHP1A adults who are GH-sufficient, consistent with GH deficiency contributing to the short stature. Although GH deficiency contributes to short stature in approximately 2/3 of patients with PHP1A, premature fusion of the epiphyses also has a large impact on final adult height, as previ ously discussed. It is important to note that although rGH treatment can increase growth velocity and height short term [34, 72, 127,

149], the long-term efficacy of rGH treatment with respect to stature can truly only be assessed once the final height has been achieved in a large cohort in the setting of premature epiphyseal closure. The effects of rGH treatment on final height in GH-deficient children with PHP1A are being assessed in a long-term prospective clinical trial that has been ongoing for close to two decades [38, 40, 150]. Given that even without GH deficiency, children with PHP1A still have a short final adult height, a longitudinal prospective study of GH-sufficient PHP1A children treated with rGH is also being analyzed in order to determine the effect on final adult height while increasing growth velocity maximally with rGH before growth plate closure [150]. ### 22.4.2.5 Calcitonin Resistance

### and Bone Mineral Density/ Bone Remodeling

Calcitonin resistance has also been reported in patients with PHP1A, although it typically does not present clinically in a manner requir ing treatment. Calcitonin resistance exhibit ing hypercalcitoninemia, both with and without pentagastrin stimulation, has been reported in isolated cases in the literature [75, 76, 160–164], but its prevalence may be higher based on the experiences of experts who took part in the international Consensus Statement for PHP and related disorders [38]. Although the effects of calcitonin resistance itself do not usually require treatment, it is important to exclude the diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Investigations in both humans and mice have revealed that regulation of bone remod eling is impacted by paternal imprinting and results in effects on bone mineral density (BMD) [77, 78, 165]. Specifically, recent evi dence from studies in an AHO mouse model [77] indicates that the parental origin of a mutant Gnas allele can differentially affect bone remodeling, with data suggesting that this may be due to partial calcitonin resistance in osteoclasts [77, 78]. Based on these studies, it appears that calcitonin resistance may potentially contribute to the bone density phenotype that has been observed in patients with PHP1A [77, 78, 165]. It had been thought in the past that these patients may be more prone to low BMD due to PTH resistance being specific to renal proximal tubules but not bone. However, it became clear based on studies in a large cohort of PHP1A patients evaluated with dual-energy x-ray absorptiom etry (DXA) scans that BMD is instead nor mal or increased and that early osteopenia/ osteoporosis is not of clinical concern [165].

Glucagon resistance has also been reported but does not have the striking features of other hormonal resistances; it is not as com mon and does not have obvious clinical conse quences. ACTH and vasopressin resistance are not seen, presumably as a result of cells that express the receptors for these hormones exhibiting biallelic expression of GNAS [28, 29, 38, 40, 41, 67, 70].

### 22.4.2.7 Obesity

Obesity in AHO had been classically described as being similar in both PHP1A and PPHP according to Fuller Albright’s original description many decades ago [1, 2]. However, approximately 15 years ago, it became clear that severe obesity is a feature solely of PHP1A [44]. Although birthweight is slightly below the mean, early-onset obesity is signifi cant and is often one of the first signs of PHP1A [34, 37–41, 44, 126, 127, 167]. There is a striking increase in BMI through the first two years of life. Severe obesity often contin ues throughout the lifespan, though seem ingly less pronounced in adulthood, with women tending to be heavier than men [34, 37, 40, 41, 44, 126].

Multiple factors have been identified that may contribute to the development of obesity in PHP1A, a major one being hypothalamic imprinting. The observation that severe obe sity is present in PHP1A but not PPHP was the first indication that imprinting may be involved [44]. Investigations in both humans and mice revealed that obesity was not due to imprinting in adipose tissue [29, 81, 84]. Further studies in mice led to the finding that paternal imprinting of Gnas in MC4Rexpressing cells of the dorsomedial hypothal amus plays a major role in the development of

obesity and that imprinting was indeed involved. In addition, these studies revealed that Gαs is necessary to control energy bal ance, thermogenesis, and peripheral glucose metabolism; however, there was no effect on food intake [82, 83]. It had previously been demonstrated that morbid obesity can be seen without evidence of hyperphagia in PHP1A patients. In addition, studies revealed that hyperphagia does not play a significant role in the rapid weight gain seen during childhood which is instead due to a decrease in resting energy expenditure [44, 168–172]. Other con tributing factors toward obesity include peripheral resistance to epinephrine, low sym pathetic nervous system activity, and decreased lipolysis [44, 173–175]. In addition, GH deficiency in approximately 2/3 of patients can contribute to the obesity phenotype in PHP1A [40, 72, 127].

Concomitant with the obesity, adults with PHP1A also exhibit higher rates of type 2 dia betes along with reduced insulin sensitivity, even compared to obese controls. This impli cates that the reduced insulin sensitivity could contribute to the pathogenesis of glucose intolerance and that obesity is not the sole cause [173]. Children with PHP1A are at high risk for dysglycemia but do not appear to have reduced insulin sensitivity; they appear to have lower hemoglobin A1c (HgbA1c) levels compared to controls [172]. Metabolic syn drome also occurs in both children and adults with PHP1A. Lipid profiles are not markedly affected [172, 176], although patients have the classic profiles observed in obesity. Most stud ies have not found an increased risk of hyper tension [169, 172, 173]. Therefore, the relationship between obesity and metabolic effects in patients with PHP1A is complex, and further investigations are clearly needed. In terms of the implications of obesity and type 2 diabetes, patients with PHP1A have a normal life expectancy [116] consistent with findings in the mouse model [29].

Treatment of obesity is one of the most challenging issues for PHP1A patients and families. Dietary management and exercise are helpful, but the decreased resting energy expenditure makes obesity very difficult to control. Exercise needs to be encouraged but

### 22.4.2.8 Craniofacial and Dental

### Abnormalities

Craniofacial abnormalities are common in patients with PHP1A [38, 40, 153, 177]. These may make them more prone to otitis media in addition to OSA, perhaps secondary to the mid-face hypoplasia, a relatively common finding [124, 151]. In fact, the “very round face” noted in the initial description of PHP by Fuller Albright [1] could be related to cra niofacial abnormalities; the face appears fuller and flatter in the setting of a smaller cranial vault and midface hypoplasia. Recent studies in a mouse model of AHO revealed a smaller cranial vault, increased cranial dome angle, and premature closure of the sphenooccipital synchondrosis (SOS), all of which are independent of the parental origin of the mutant allele [153]. It is known that prema ture SOS closure can lead to midface hypopla sia in a variety of syndromes and that it correlates directly with the severity [178–181]; this could also be a factor in the craniofacial findings in AHO. Craniosynostosis can also be a complication in PHP1A [37, 38, 40, 41, 153], and it is known to be associated with premature SOS fusion [179, 181].

In addition, Chiari malformation type 1 (CM1) is observed in PHP1A and can be an issue that leads to significant neurologic sequelae [37, 38, 40–42, 153]. Specifically, a

The abnormal cranial devel opment in the AHO mouse model as previ ously described provides a potential etiology for this increased prevalence of CM1/lowlying cerebellar tonsils [153]. Specifically, cra nial hyperostosis is a prominent feature in PHP1A, even commented on extensively in Albright’s first description in which the authors noted “marked density of the skull.” [1, 38, 40, 129, 153] This cranial hyperostosis, which had been demonstrated to be second ary to increased osteogenesis in the AHO mouse model, was observed only when the Gnas mutation was inherited maternally, con sistent with imprinting [153]. Given the increased prevalence of CM1, it is important to monitor patients with PHP1A for potential neurological signs and symp toms, especially because early interventions can improve outcomes greatly. ### 22.4.2.10 CNS: Cognitive/Behavioral

### and Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities

Cognitive issues were noted within the initial description of patients with PHP1A (then referred to as PHP) by Albright and col leagues in 1942. In 1986, Farfel and Friedman reported that cognitive impairment was asso ciated with reductions in Gαs levels in patients with PHP1A affected with intellectual disabil ity [201]. Over the ensuing years, further stud ies demonstrated that as many as 79% of patients with PHP1A have cognitive impair ment [38, 202]. In general, it is now estimated that at least 1/2 to 2/3 of patients with PHP1A are affected, ranging from minimal to severe learning disabilities [34, 37, 38, 40, 43, 203–205] often requiring early interventions and therapies in grade school and beyond [34, 40, 204, 205]. Studies of children with PHP1A have revealed lower IQ scores (full scale, non verbal, and verbal) and impaired behavioral, adaptive, attention, and/or executive function, along with both verbal and nonverbal com promise; in addition, ADHD and autism spectrum disorders are common in PHP1A and can compromise learning and social func

In general, patients with PHP1A have a wide range of functioning in school during childhood, affected by both the cogni tive and behavioral issues. Various levels of education are completed depending on the degree of dysfunction, and individualized educational plans are very common [40, 205].

Patients with PPHP appear to have overall higher educational and social functioning as adults than those with PHP1A [40]. Cognitive testing in a single kindred with AHO showed that PHP1A family members were more affected than those with PPHP [202], although this study was limited by a small cohort and by the use of a single measure for cognitive function. Specific CNS abnormalities, such as with olfaction, hearing, and taste, have also been reported in PHP1A patients and are not present in PPHP patients [206–209], thereby raising the possibility that imprinting could be involved. In addition, mothering behavior has been shown to be impaired in mice carry ing a Gnas deletion on their maternally inher ited allele (PHP1A) but not in mice carrying a paternally inherited mutant Gnas allele (PPHP) [29, 34]. All of these studies suggest an important role for paternal imprinting in the CNS for which further investigation is needed comparing cognitive and behavioral function in PHP1A versus PPHP [150].

The impact on cognition and behavior in PHP1A can be one of the most difficult aspects of this disorder for both the patients and their families. Early intervention pro grams are extremely important, as are appro priate developmental evaluations and rehabilitation involvement, such as with occupational, physical, and speech therapies [205]. This is especially the case in light of underlying issues with fine and gross motor delay as well as speech apraxia [40, 125, 204, 205]. Hypotonia is noted in some children and can lead to gross motor delay. Once in school, it is important to have educational support with individual educational and learning plans as needed. ### 22.4.2.11 Transition to Adult Care

Transition to adult care is an especially diffi cult time for patients with PHP1A. It is hard to find specialists in the field, and work should be done ahead of time so that there is a smooth transition. Some clinics allow the pediatric specialist to follow the patient into adulthood, but plans need to be made well ahead if this will not be possible in order to transition to another healthcare provider. In PHP1A, part of the provider’s role is to advo cate for help with disability issues and support of activities of daily living when no longer under their parents’ care. In fact, the concern about independent living is one of the greatest that families have on a daily basis [40]. Many patients with the disorder live with their fami lies long-term or transition to group homes. They can have difficulty completing high school and only occasionally attend college depending on the level of learning disability. There can also be difficulty in maintaining jobs. The medical provider can provide sup port in laying out appropriate guidelines for educational choices and part-time job place ments that can help to achieve gradual inde pendence along with the help of the school, employer, and social work. Over the past decade, there have been an increasing number of colleges and jobs that provide a great deal of support to help patients with cognitive and social challenges, typically requiring a letter from the provider on the specific disabilities involved. In this regard, advocacy is a very important part of the clinical management of

PHP1A in order to maximize the quality of life for these patients [38, 40, 210].

### 22.4.3 Pseudohypoparathyroidism

### Type 1C (PHP1C): iPPSD2, OMIM #612462

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1C (PHP1C) presents identically to PHP1A, but the AHO features are generally milder. PHP1C is due to mutations that affect receptor coupling of Gαs, specifically thought to be due to mutations in exon 13 (last exon) of the maternally derived GNAS allele [26, 38, 40–43]. Testing to separate PHP1C from PHP1A is impractical, and it has been proposed that PHP1C be removed from the nomenclature [37, 38, 40–42]. The manage ment is the same as for PHP1A.

### 22.4.4 Pseudopseudohypoparathy

### roidism (PPHP): iPPSD2, OMIM #612463

PPHP patients have the clinical phenotype of AHO involving brachydactyly, adult short stature, and SCOs, although all three of these features do not need to be present in order to make the diagnosis. This condition has been discussed in detail in the previous sections. An important feature to note is that infants with PPHP are often born SGA [80], which can be a helpful sign in overall clinical diagnosis. Recombinant GH treatment can be consid ered for the FDA-approved indication of SGA if the patient meets the appropriate cri teria, but there are no published data at pres ent in terms of the impact on height.

Because hormonal resistance and brachy dactyly are often absent clinically in infants and young children with PHP1A, it is difficult to discriminate PPHP from PHP1A at these early ages. For example, this is the case if the diagno sis is based on the finding of SCOs. Patients with PHP1B also have an increased BMI in childhood, and they are overweight/obese as adults but not as severe as for PHP1A. Final height does not seem to be compromised (and if so, minimally), although there can be a shortened or absent pubertal growth spurt [126, 212]. ### 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis

As described in the preceding sections, the spectrum of pseudohypoparathyroidism and related disorders comprises a group of condi tions that have a unique yet overlapping set of clinical phenotypes. Additionally, many of these disorders have clinical signs, symptoms, and biochemical/hormonal profiles that change over the lifespan. In many cases, the diagnosis of these disorders can be narrowed down significantly based on family history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and imaging even before performing mutation analysis. However, as is evident throughout this chapter, patients with PHP and related disorders can have findings consistent with more than one condition. Therefore, genetic testing can be quite helpful in several respects.

First, in some cases, the clinical diagnosis can be inconclusive. This especially pertains to PHP and related disorders since the range


## PDF page 596 | printed page 590

of phenotypes can be variable, both in terms of the age of onset of clinical and laboratory features as well as the severity of signs and symptoms. As discussed earlier, patients can sometimes be given a diagnosis consistent with one disorder, which is subsequently amended as additional clinical features develop or become apparent over time. Therefore, identification of the specific genetic alteration is important in order to confirm the diagnosis of the patient. Second, knowing the specific mutation can provide information for current and future family members since tar geted testing for the specific region of the affected gene can be performed if needed for their own evaluations or future evaluations; this saves both time and money as well. In this respect, prenatal diagnosis is also possible, and collaborations with geneticists and genetic counselors can be very helpful. Third, and important going forward into the future, genetic testing can reveal the severity of the mutation, which can be useful in a general sense in anticipating the severity of certain clinical features based on genotype-phenotype correlations, such as the correlation observed with subcutaneous ossifications [100]. Although genotype-phenotype correlations are not available for many of the clinical issues observed in PHP and related disorders, more of these correlations may evolve with the greater availability and sophistication of molecular testing over the past decade and with scientific investigations continually advancing.

Genetic testing for diagnostic purposes is available for most of the PHP and related dis orders in multiple commercial CLIAapproved laboratories through targeted testing and sequencing of key genes, such as GNAS, PRKAR1A, PDE4D, and PDE3A, that are discussed in this chapter (for review, [38–43]). Methylation analysis, as well as test ing for STX16 deletions to confirm the diag nosis of PHP1B, can also be performed in CLIA-approved laboratories, although meth ylation testing is not always routinely avail able. A small percentage of sporadic PHP1B is due to patUPD20q, which can also be assessed. If determination of the parental ori

### 22

gin of the mutant allele is important for diag nostic purposes, a simple approach is to perform genetic testing on the parents or other family members. In cases in which this is not possible due to adoption or spontaneous mutations, analysis of the parental origin of the mutation from patient RNA can be per formed in a research laboratory for investiga tional purposes. Finally, although there are instances in which the diagnosis of these dis orders is identified by whole exome (or genome) sequencing, these tests are not typi cally needed for diagnostic purposes if a thor ough clinical workup has been completed, including a detailed history, physical examina tion, and laboratory/radiologic evaluation. However, on occasion, these more extensive analyses are truly necessary and can prove to be quite helpful.

### 22.5 Summary

Remarkable advances have been made toward understanding the mechanisms underlying the PHP spectrum ever since its initial descrip tion by Fuller Albright and colleagues approximately eight decades ago. Through both clinical and laboratory investigations, the phenotypes have been elucidated in more detail, and the mechanisms of the multiple clinical issues have been unfolding, such as for the multihormone resistance, adult short stat ure, brachydactyly, subcutaneous ossifica tions, obesity and metabolic disturbances, craniofacial and dental abnormalities, aber rant bone regulation, and cognitive/behav ioral impairments that are often a part of these conditions. As more knowledge has continually been gained from clinical and lab oratory investigations, the diagnosis, treat ment, and management for these patients have improved immensely, as has the aware ness of these conditions overall. Due to the evolving nature of the clinical issues in PHP and related disorders as well as their complex ities, constant attention to early intervention, close follow-up, and long-term management is key to the overall health and quality of life for patients with these conditions.
